In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

text.text: There is growing recognition of the importance of designing work environments that promote the well-being of diverse employees.

Although the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model has contributed substantially to work engagement research, there remains scope to extend it to address the challenge of creating inclusive work environments.
We examined the associations of workplace tolerance and individual autonomy with work engagement, including the potential mediating roles of psychological safety and intrinsic motivation.
We used data from 1084 Japanese workers collected across four waves of online surveys and conducted causal mediation analyses.

As a result, the presence of tolerant coworkers was associated with work engagement through workplace psychological safety (total effect = 0.296; proportion mediated = 29.7 %), whereas the absence of intolerant coworkers was not clearly associated with work engagement.
Individual autonomy was also associated with work engagement through intrinsic motivation (total effect = 0.444), although the proportion mediated was modest (14.5 %).

These findings suggest that positioning workplace tolerance and individual autonomy as social and personal resources, respectively, may extend the JD-R model by enabling it to describe the conditions under which employees with diverse characteristics and circumstances can engage in their work on an equitable basis.
Contemporary societies are experiencing declining birth rates and population aging simultaneously, and these demographic changes are contributing to a shrinking workforce.
At the same time, populations are becoming increasingly diverse.

Against this background, there is growing recognition of the importance of designing work environments that prioritize the well-being of diverse individuals alongside conventional outcomes such as labor productivity (Cabinet Office, Government of Japan, 2019; Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, 2024; OECD, 2020).

In response to these demographic changes and the accompanying needs to secure an adequate workforce and promote equity, organizational psychology and management research have accumulated a substantial body of knowledge and practice concerning work engagement and diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI).
Work engagement is defined as "a positive, fulfilling, work-related state of mind that is characterized by vigor, dedication, and absorption" (Schaufeli et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Work engagement is defined as "a positive, fulfilling, work-related state of mind that is characterized by vigor, dedication, and absorption" <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Schaufeli et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Work engagement has been associated with employees' health and well-being, including psychological distress and life satisfaction, as well as important work-related outcomes such as job satisfaction, organizational commitment, turnover intentions, and productivity (Eguchi et al., 2015 (Eguchi et al., , 2020;; Halbesleben, 2010; Kuroda et al., 2021; Mazzetti et al., 2023; Shimazu et al., 2008).

text.text: Thus, work engagement is not only a component of well-being that is worth pursuing in its own right but is also associated with a range of important organizational outcomes.
The Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model is a central framework in the work engagement research (Bakker et al., 2023; Hakanen & Roodt, 2010; Schaufeli & Bakker, 2004).

text.text: Within this model, resources are aspects of work or the individual that facilitate goal attainment, help employees manage job demands, and promote personal growth and development (Bakker et al., 2023).

text.text: These include social, work-related, developmental, and personal resources (Mazzetti et al., 2023).

text.text: However, the JD-R model has developed primarily by examining how job demands and resources influence motivational and health-related outcomes.
It has paid comparatively less attention to identifying resources that enable employees with diverse characteristics and circumstances to engage in their work on an equitable basis.

Thus, although the JD-R model has contributed to addressing organizational concerns such as workforce sustainability and productivity, there remains scope to extend it to address the challenge of creating work environments in which diverse individuals have equitable opportunities to achieve well-being.

A substantial body of research has also examined the DEI in organizational contexts. Cox and Blake (1991) established a perspective that regards diversity management not as a cost or obligation but as a strategic organizational resource. Shore et al. (2011) conceptually distinguished diversity from inclusion and defined workplace inclusion as a state in which employees' needs for both belongingness and uniqueness are satisfied.

text.text: Thus, diversity management requires more than increasing demographic representation through recruitment and promotion; increasing attention has been paid to whether everyday interactions and workplace environments create inclusive conditions that enable employees to participate and contribute fully (Ely & Thomas, 2020; Mor Barak, 2015; Shore et al., 2018).

text.text: Despite the growing recognition of the importance of inclusion, limitations in current DEI practices have also been identified.
Organizational practice has tended to emphasize the implementation of discrete programs, such as training, mentoring, networking initiatives, and grievance procedures.
However, these initiatives may fail to produce sustained change and can sometimes have unintended adverse consequences (Benschop et al., 2016; Dobbin & Kalev, 2017; Ely & Thomas, 2020; Leslie, 2019).

text.text: In response to these concerns, attention has increasingly shifted from simply asking what programs have been implemented to examining how DEI initiatives can transform workplace learning, psychological safety, and power structures.

Implementation gaps-including the lack of interventions tailored to organizational needs through processes such as needs assessment and the oversimplification of evaluation metrics-have also been identified as important challenges (Ely & Thomas, 2020; Roberson, 2019).

text.text: Against these backgrounds, researchers working in Japan have introduced a new perspective on inclusion from outside the conventional contexts of organizational psychology.

Drawing on discussions in political theory (Galston, 2005; Hobhouse, 1911 Hobhouse, /2010;; Raz, 1988), Costantini et al. (2024) and Ono et al. (2026a) focused on the concepts of tolerance and autonomy as conditions for enabling diverse individuals to achieve well-being.

text.text: Ono et al.
(2026a) defined tolerance as "respecting, caring, and accommodating diverse individuals within a society to maintain or enhance their well-being."
Autonomy, by contrast, was defined as "an individual agency that balances one's dependence portfolio for one's own well-being."

Based on these definitions, Ono et al. (2026a) developed self-administered questionnaire scales assessing the extent to which individuals are surrounded by tolerant people and the extent to which they exercise autonomy.

text.text: They also found that being surrounded by more tolerant people and having greater autonomy were associated with higher well-being, and these associations were broadly consistent among diverse people.
These findings suggest that fostering tolerance within society and enhancing individual autonomy may be important for achieving well-being in a society characterized by diversity.

Although Ono et al. (2026a), examined tolerance and autonomy in the context of social life in general, their conceptualization may offer a means of extending the JD-R model to better address the demand for equity.

Positioning workplace tolerance and individual autonomy within the JD-R model would bring the conditions required to create inclusive workplaces-where people with diverse characteristics and circumstances can engage in their work-within the scope of the model.
Accordingly, we proposed the following hypotheses: Hypothesis 1: Workplace tolerance is associated with work engagement.
Hypothesis 2: Individual autonomy is associated with work engagement.

text.text: As described below, T0, T1, T2, and T3 denote the time points at which the surveys were conducted, corresponding to the baseline survey and the three followup surveys, respectively.
Data from four online surveys were used in this study.
The baseline survey was conducted in March 2025, followed by three follow-up surveys at six-month intervals.
For the baseline survey, 2500 participants were recruited from a survey company's panel of approximately 13 million registered individuals.

Quotas were established for 22 strata defined by age (11 five-year age groups ranging from 15-19 to 65-69 years) and sex (men and women) so that the sample distribution would correspond to that of Japan's employed population.
The distribution of the employed population was calculated by the authors using data from the Japanese Labour Force Survey for October 2024.
The baseline survey was conducted on March 13, 2025.
In every survey, informed consent was obtained electronically from all participants prior to participation.

Specifically, participants were required to carefully read the study description and indicate their consent by checking a designated box; only those who provided consent were allowed to proceed to the questionnaire.

Participants who failed some attention-check items at baseline were excluded from followup because their responses were considered indicative of satisficing-that is, responding with insufficient attention or effort in an attempt to complete the survey quickly.
Satisficing has been reported to bias indicators of reliability and validity (Hamby & Taylor, 2016).
text.formatted: Satisficing has been reported to bias indicators of reliability and validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Hamby & Taylor, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The attention check questions were specially designed items for which a specific correct option could be identified if the question was read attentively.
Three follow-up surveys were conducted at six-month intervals after the baseline survey: the first in September 2025, the second in March 2026, and the third in September 2026.
In this article, the baseline survey is denoted as T0, and the three follow-up surveys are denoted as T1, T2, and T3, respectively.

A change in workplace during the follow-up period would make it difficult to appropriately examine the associations between workplace tolerance or individual autonomy and the mediators and outcomes assessed at subsequent time points.
Therefore, at each follow-up survey, participants were asked whether their primary workplace had changed since T0.
The primary analyses were restricted to participants who did not change their primary workplace at the third follow-up survey.
Details of the item used to assess workplace change are provided in Supplementary material 1.
Participants younger than 18 years were also excluded from the final analyses because working conditions and the social and legal context of employment differ between minors and adults.
Although individuals younger than 18 years participated in the baseline and follow-up surveys, they were excluded from the final analytical sample.
We adapted the Tolerance of Surroundings Scale (TSS) developed by Ono et al. (2026a) to assess perceived tolerance in the workplace.

text.text: The original TSS is a valid and reliable selfadministered instrument that assesses the extent to which respondents perceive themselves as being surrounded by tolerant and intolerant people at the micro and meso levels.
Although the micro-level component of the original scale encompasses coworkers, the present study required a measure specifically focused on the workplace.

Moreover, if the tolerance of surrounding people is considered a potential target of organizational intervention, organizations have limited capacity to influence people outside an employee's workplace.
We therefore modified the introductory instructions and item wording by changing the referent from "people around you" to "coworkers."
Details of the adapted scale, hereafter referred to as the Workplace Tolerance Scale, are provided in Supplementary material 1.
The Workplace Tolerance Scale consists of 10 items representing two factors: the presence of tolerant coworkers (PTCW) and the absence of intolerant coworkers (AICW).
In the present study, we examined its two-factor structural validity and internal consistency using the T0 and T1 data.
The results supported the proposed two-factor structure and demonstrated good internal consistency for both subscales.
Details of these analyses are provided in Supplementary material 1.
Subscale scores were calculated by summing the corresponding item scores.
The PTCW score ranges from 0 to 16, with higher scores indicating that the respondent is surrounded by more tolerant coworkers.
The AICW score ranges from 0 to 24, with higher scores indicating that the respondent is surrounded by fewer intolerant coworkers.
We used the 12-item version of the Autonomy Scale developed by Ono et al. (2026b).

text.text: This scale is a valid and reliable self-administered instrument comprising three factors: selfdependence in decision-making and practice, interdependence with others, and selfdependence in emotion and cognition.
The scope of individual behavior assessed by this scale is not restricted to the workplace; therefore, the scale was administered in its original form.

This decision was based on the premise that, when individual autonomy is considered a potential target of organizational intervention, organizations may support employees' autonomy both within and outside the workplace through employee support and benefit programs.
In the present study, the autonomy score was calculated by summing the 12 item scores.

The total score ranges from 0 to 36, with higher scores indicating a greater capacity to maintain personal agency in decision-making, role performance, and the regulation of emotions and thoughts while also being able to rely on others.

text.text: We conducted causal mediation analyses as the primary analyses to estimate the average causal mediation effect (ACME), average direct effect (ADE), total effect, and proportion mediated.
In each analysis, the exposure was measured at T1, the mediator at T2, and work engagement at T3.
The models were adjusted for the mediator and work engagement measured at T0, as well as the prespecified individual-and workplace-level control variables measured at T0.

As supplementary analyses, we used inverse probability-of-censoring-weighted linear regression to examine the associations of the T1 exposures with work engagement and workaholism at T3 while accounting for potential selection bias due to loss to follow-up.
Missing data were handled using multiple imputation under the missing-at-random assumption and estimates from 30 imputed datasets were pooled using Rubin's rules.
All analyses used the original score metrics without standardization or normalization.

text.text: Turning first to workplace tolerance, the findings partially supported Hypotheses 1 and 3.
The total effect of the PTCW score was 0.296, and the estimated proportion mediated was 29.7%.
The 95%CIs for both the ACME and ADE excluded zero.
In contrast, although the estimated proportion mediated for the AICW score was 29.6 %, its total effect was 0.066, with a 95%CI that included zero.
Thus, PTCW was associated with work engagement through psychological safety, whereas AICW was not clearly associated with work engagement.
The supplementary regression analyses yielded consistent findings: the PTCW score was associated with the work engagement, whereas the AICW score was not.
Accordingly, Hypotheses 1 and 3 were partially supported in that PTCW was associated with work engagement through workplace psychological safety, whereas AICW was not associated with work engagement.
For individual autonomy, the total effect was 0.444, and the estimated proportion mediated was 14.5 %.
The 95%CIs for both the ACME and ADE excluded zero.
The supplementary regression analysis also showed an association of a similar magnitude between individual autonomy and work engagement.
These findings indicate that individual autonomy was associated with work engagement through intrinsic motivation.
However, the proportion of the association mediated by intrinsic motivation was modest.

Thus, Hypotheses 2 and 4 were supported in that individual autonomy was associated with work engagement partly through intrinsic motivation, although the contribution of this mediating pathway was relatively limited.

The principal theoretical contribution of this study lies in positioning workplace tolerance and individual autonomy as a social resource and a personal resource, respectively, within the JD-R model and examining their longitudinal associations with work engagement.

The findings showed that the PTCW and autonomy scores were associated with work engagement through psychological safety and intrinsic motivation, respectively-existing constructs that are related to the two proposed resources.
However, these mediating pathways accounted for only 29.7% and 14.5% of the respective total associations.

These findings suggest that workplace tolerance and individual autonomy, although related to proximal established constructs such as psychological safety and intrinsic motivation, may capture resources that are not fully reducible to those constructs.

Incorporating tolerance and autonomy as social and personal resources may enable the JD-R model to describe more explicitly the conditions under which employees with diverse characteristics and circumstances can engage in their work on an equitable basis.
Extending the JD-R model in this way may also provide a conceptual basis for assessing inclusion-related conditions at both the social and individual levels.

Specifically, the PTCW and individual autonomy scores may serve as complementary dimensions capturing a social resource within the work environment and a personal resource through which employees manage their relationships with others.
Used together, these dimensions may support organizational needs assessment and the tailoring of interventions to the specific needs of each organization.

This approach may help address implementation gaps in DEI practice, including the limited adaptation of interventions to organizational needs and the reliance on overly simplified evaluation metrics (Ely & Thomas, 2020; Roberson, 2019).

text.text: However, the present study did not examine whether the distributions of workplace tolerance and individual autonomy or their associations with work engagement differed across employee subgroups.

Such heterogeneity should not be investigated solely by dividing participants into broad categories such as older employees, people with disabilities, parents, family caregivers, or LGBTQ+ individuals.

Rather, future studies should define theoretically meaningful subgroups based on relevant configurations of individual characteristics, job demands, and resources and ensure adequate sample sizes within each group.

Such investigations would help clarify more concretely how incorporating workplace tolerance and individual autonomy into the JD-R model can contribute to understanding and assessing equitable and inclusive work environments.
This study was a longitudinal observational study in which the exposures were modeled as continuous variables.

Therefore, before these findings can be translated into workplace practice, interventions targeting workplace tolerance and individual autonomy must be developed and evaluated in experimental studies.
Nevertheless, the present findings offer implications for the design and practical application of such future studies.

First, the finding that the PTCW score was associated with work engagement whereas the AICW score was not suggests that, specifically for promoting work engagement, increasing tolerant behaviors among employees may be more important than merely reducing intolerant behaviors.

More specifically, promoting tolerant behaviors-such as respecting diverse perspectives, helping one another, and adapting one's behavior in response to others' requests-may be particularly important, in addition to discouraging intolerant behaviors such as discriminatory conduct or the rejection of diversity.
However, AICW might have relevance within particular subgroups, including groups that have historically experienced discrimination.
This possibility further underscores the value of conducting stratified analyses in theoretically meaningful groups as discussed above.
Second, the concept of individual autonomy adopted in this study may offer a perspective on work engagement that differs from autonomy as conceptualized in self-determination theory.
The concept proposed by Ono et al. (2026a) refers to a state in which individuals can combine a sense of personal ownership over their decisions and actions with the ability to rely on others.

Although this approach must be evaluated in studies designed to estimate its causal effects more rigorously, an approach based on a concept of autonomy that incorporates not only self-determination but also reliance on others may support employees' needs for both belongingness and uniqueness (Shore et al., 2011), thereby contributing to the creation of more inclusive workplaces.

This study has several limitations.
First, participants were recruited from a panel maintained by an online survey company.
Although recruitment quotas were used to align the age and sex distribution of the sample with that of Japan's working population, the possibility of sampling bias cannot be excluded.
Therefore, when generalizing the findings, differences between the study participants and the target population to which the findings are applied should be carefully considered.

Second, although we used statistical procedures to adjust for potential confounders and selection bias, these procedures do not necessarily establish that the estimated associations represent causal effects.
We also assumed treatment-version irrelevance-that different ways of attaining the same exposure score would not result in different outcomes.
In addition, the exposures were modeled as continuous variables, and linear relationships between the exposures and outcomes were assumed.
Given their dependence on these assumptions, the findings should be interpreted as covariate-adjusted longitudinal associations rather than causal effects.
Third, the estimated associations may remain affected by common method bias.
To mitigate this risk, we used scales with established content validity, avoided ambiguous wording, administered the survey anonymously, and allowed respondents to leave questions unanswered.
In addition, the control variables, exposures, mediators, and outcomes were measured at different time points.

These procedures may have reduced social desirability bias, response pressure, and shared covariance arising from simultaneous measurement, thereby limiting common method bias to some extent (Podsakoff et al., 2003).

text.text: Nevertheless, the exclusive use of self-report questionnaires remains a limitation.

Using data from four waves of online surveys, this study examined the associations of workplace tolerance and individual autonomy with work engagement, including the potential mediating roles of psychological safety and intrinsic motivation.
PTCW was associated with work engagement through workplace psychological safety, whereas AICW was not associated with work engagement.
Individual autonomy was also associated with work engagement through intrinsic motivation, although the proportion mediated by intrinsic motivation was modest.

The findings suggest that positioning workplace tolerance and individual autonomy as social and personal resources, respectively, may extend the JD-R model by enabling it to describe the conditions under which employees with diverse characteristics and circumstances can engage in their work on an equitable basis.

Future research should define theoretically meaningful subgroups and examine the distributions of workplace tolerance and individual autonomy and their associations with work engagement within these groups.
Interventions targeting workplace tolerance and individual autonomy should also be developed and evaluated in future experimental studies.

At T0, Cronbach's alpha values for the Presence of tolerant coworkers (PTCW) and absence of intolerant coworkers (AICW) subscales were 0.83 (95% CI: 0.83-0.85) and 0.86 (95% CI: 0.85-0.87), respectively.
At T1, the corresponding values were 0.88 (95% CI: 0.87-0.89) and 0.89 (95% CI: 0.88-0.90), respectively.
These findings support the structural validity and internal consistency reliability of the workplace tolerance scale.

text.text: We used the Workplace Psychological Safety Scale developed by O'Donovan et al. (2020).
text.formatted: We used the Workplace Psychological Safety Scale developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">O'Donovan et al. (2020)</ref>.

text.text: This self-administered instrument assesses psychological safety in the respondent's workplace and consists of nine items concerning the team leader, seven items concerning coworkers or other team members, and three items concerning the team as a whole.
The validity and reliability of the Japanese version were demonstrated by Sasaki et al. (2022).
text.formatted: The validity and reliability of the Japanese version were demonstrated by <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Sasaki et al. (2022)</ref>.

text.text: Because this study focused on the association between workplace tolerance and work engagement, we considered psychological safety in relation to coworkers and the team as a whole to be the components most relevant to the hypothesized mediation mechanism.
We also considered that some respondents might work in settings without an identifiable team leader or might themselves serve as team leaders.
Therefore, the present survey used the seven items concerning coworkers or other team members and the three items concerning the team as a whole.
The scores for these 10 items were summed to calculate the psychological safety score (PS score) used in the analyses.
We used the Short Work Extrinsic and Intrinsic Motivation Scale.
The scale assesses respondents' motivation toward work.

Although the original version developed by Tremblay et al. (2009) consists of 18 items, a Japanese version and a shortened 12-item version were subsequently developed (Kotera et al., 2022 (Kotera et al., , 2024)).
text.formatted: Although the original version developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Tremblay et al. (2009)</ref> consists of 18 items, a Japanese version and a shortened 12-item version were subsequently developed <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Kotera et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kotera et al., , 2024))</ref>.

text.text: The Japanese version has a three-factor structure and has demonstrated good internal consistency.
Although all 12 items were administered in the present survey, only the eight items assessing intrinsic motivation were used in the analyses.
The mean for these eight items was used as the intrinsic motivation score (IM score).
We used the nine-item version of the Utrecht Work Engagement Scale (UWES; Schaufeli et al., 2002).
text.formatted: We used the nine-item version of the Utrecht Work Engagement Scale (UWES; <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Schaufeli et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: The UWES assesses three dimensions of work engagement: vigor, dedication, and absorption.
The original 17-item version has been used in 32 countries and is among the most widely used instruments in work-engagement research.
In the present study, we used the nine-item version, which contains three items for each dimension.
A validated Japanese version of the nine-item UWES is available and has demonstrated satisfactory reliability and validity (Shimazu et al., 2008).
text.formatted: A validated Japanese version of the nine-item UWES is available and has demonstrated satisfactory reliability and validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Shimazu et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The scores for all nine items were summed to calculate the UWES score used in the analyses.

Although measuring work engagement was sufficient to address the primary objectives of this study, previous research has emphasized the importance of distinguishing work engagement from workaholism, which is characterized by compulsive and excessive working (Shimazu et al., 2009 (Shimazu et al., , 2012 (Shimazu et al., , 2015)).

text.text: An approach toward inclusive workplace should contribute to employees working with energy and fulfillment without promoting compulsive or excessive working.
It was therefore important to examine whether workplace tolerance and individual autonomy were associated with work engagement but not with workaholism.
Accordingly, workaholism was included as a supplementary outcome.
Workaholism was assessed using the Dutch Workaholism Scale (DUWAS; Schaufeli et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Workaholism was assessed using the Dutch Workaholism Scale (DUWAS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Schaufeli et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The DUWAS consists of 10 items representing two factors: working excessively and working compulsively.
The total score ranges from 10 to 40, with higher scores indicating a stronger tendency to work excessively and compulsively.
A Japanese version of the DUWAS was developed by Schaufeli et al. (2009).
